subject: ela
intro: Each problem includes a full informational passage that develops one subject in several stages. Read it closely, then trace how the author introduces, illustrates, and elaborates that subject across the whole text. Name the author's moves (introduce, illustrate, elaborate) and show how the parts connect, rather than just retelling what the passage says.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"In 1845, a doctor named Ignaz Semmelweis worked in a hospital where many new mothers died of a fever soon after giving birth. The numbers troubled him. In one ward, run by doctors, far more women died than in a second ward, run by midwives. The two wards treated the same kinds of patients, so the gap made no sense to him. Semmelweis searched for the difference between them. The doctors, he noticed, often came straight from examining dead bodies to deliver babies, while the midwives did not. He guessed that something invisible was carried from the bodies to the patients on the doctors' hands. In 1847, he ordered the doctors to scrub their hands in a chlorine solution before each delivery. The death rate in their ward dropped sharply within months. Yet most doctors refused to believe him, partly because he could not name the invisible cause, and partly because they were offended by the idea that their own hands had spread death. Semmelweis died years later, his work mocked. Only after his death, when scientists proved that germs cause disease, was he finally honored as a man who had seen the truth too early."

Trace how the author develops the subject of Semmelweis from introduction to conclusion. Name the stages and show how each part builds on the one before.
items.answer: The author introduces Semmelweis as a doctor disturbed by mothers dying of fever (introduction). The author then illustrates the puzzle with the comparison between the doctors' ward and the midwives' ward, which had different death rates (illustration). Next the author elaborates by showing Semmelweis noticing the doctors came from dead bodies, guessing at an invisible cause, and ordering handwashing, which lowered the death rate. The author deepens the portrait by adding the doctors' refusal and his lonely death, then ends by elaborating his legacy: he was honored only after germs were proven real. Each stage builds on the last, moving from a troubling problem, to a tested solution, to a tragic but vindicated legacy.

steps: Identify the subject the text develops: the doctor Ignaz Semmelweis.
Find the introduction: he is presented as troubled by mothers dying of fever.
Find the illustration: the contrast between the doctors' ward and the midwives' ward shows the puzzle concretely.
Find the elaboration: his observation, his guess about an invisible cause, the handwashing order, and the falling death rate build the idea.
Find the deepening and conclusion: the doctors' rejection, his death, and his later vindication extend the portrait.
Connect the stages: each part builds on the one before, moving from problem to solution to legacy.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

"The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is not the floating island of trash many people imagine. It is something stranger and harder to fix. The patch sits in a vast region of the North Pacific where ocean currents spin in a slow circle, pulling floating debris toward the center. Most of what gathers there is not bottles and crates but tiny flecks of broken-down plastic, some no larger than a grain of rice. These flecks spread through the water like a thin soup that no boat can simply scoop up. Sunlight and waves grind larger plastics into these pieces over many years. Fish and seabirds mistake the flecks for food and swallow them, and the plastic passes up the food chain. Because the pieces are so small and so widely scattered, cleaning the patch is far harder than removing a solid mass would be. Scientists now warn that the best answer is not a giant net but stopping plastic from reaching the ocean in the first place."

The author opens by saying the patch is "not the floating island of trash many people imagine." Explain how the rest of the passage builds on that opening sentence to develop the reader's understanding. Connect the opening to a later part.
items.answer: The opening sentence sets up a correction by saying the patch is not a floating island of trash. The author then builds on that opening by illustrating what the patch actually is: tiny flecks of broken-down plastic spread like a thin soup, some no bigger than a grain of rice. This later description directly develops the opening, because it replaces the wrong picture (a solid island) with the true one (scattered tiny pieces). The author elaborates further by explaining that these small, scattered pieces make cleanup far harder than removing a solid mass, which is the whole point the opening was preparing the reader to understand.

steps: Read the opening as a setup: it tells the reader what the patch is NOT.
Find where the author says what the patch actually is: tiny flecks of plastic spread like a thin soup.
Show the connection: the later description corrects the false image the opening named.
Trace the elaboration: the small, scattered pieces make cleanup hard, which is the understanding the opening pointed toward.

Read the passage, then answer.

"For centuries, mapmakers drew the world's coastlines but left huge blanks where the deep ocean lay. No one knew what the sea floor looked like because no one could see it. In the 1950s, a geologist named Marie Tharp began turning columns of depth readings into drawings of the ocean floor. Ships had crossed the Atlantic firing sound pulses downward and timing the echoes, and these numbers piled up in notebooks. Tharp plotted them, point by point, and a hidden landscape appeared on her paper: a giant mountain range running down the middle of the Atlantic, split by a deep valley along its crest. That valley, she argued, was a crack where the sea floor was pulling apart. At first a senior colleague dismissed her idea as 'girl talk.' But as more data filled in the same valley around the globe, her maps became impossible to ignore. They helped convince scientists that the continents really do drift, a theory many had long rejected. Tharp's patient plotting had turned a blank space on the map into evidence that reshaped how we understand the planet."

The passage develops the subject of Marie Tharp through several stages. Explain how the paragraph deepens from her quiet work to a planet-changing result, and show how the parts connect.
items.answer: The author introduces Tharp as a geologist who turned depth readings into drawings of the ocean floor, set against centuries of blank maps. The author illustrates her method: ships fired sound pulses and timed echoes, and she plotted these numbers point by point. The text then deepens by showing what appeared: a giant mountain range with a deep valley, which she argued was a crack where the sea floor pulls apart. It deepens further by adding resistance (a colleague's dismissal) and then resolution (more data confirming the valley worldwide). The final stage connects her patient plotting to a planet-changing result: her maps helped prove the continents drift. Each part builds on the last, moving from blank maps, to careful method, to discovery, to a theory that reshaped science.

steps: Name the subject: the geologist Marie Tharp.
Locate the introduction: she turned depth readings into drawings against a backdrop of blank maps.
Locate the illustration of method: ships' sound pulses and her point-by-point plotting.
Trace the deepening: the hidden mountain range and valley, her crack hypothesis, the dismissal, and the confirming data.
Connect to the result: her maps helped prove continental drift, the planet-changing payoff.
Show the chain: each stage builds toward the final understanding.

Read the passage, then answer.

"Honeybees do not speak, yet a returning forager can tell her hivemates exactly where to find flowers. She does it with a dance. Back in the dark hive, the bee runs a tight figure-eight pattern on the honeycomb while the others crowd around her. The straight middle run of the figure-eight points the way: its angle against the vertical comb matches the angle of the food against the sun outside. The longer the bee waggles during that straight run, the farther away the flowers are. So a long waggle means a long flight, and a short waggle means the food is close. The dance even adjusts as the sun moves across the sky, so the directions stay correct through the day. Scientists who decoded this dance in the 1940s were stunned that an insect could pass along such precise information without a single word."

The passage develops one central subject. Identify it, then explain how the author moves from introducing it to illustrating exactly how it works.
items.answer: The central subject is the honeybee's waggle dance, the way bees communicate where flowers are. The author introduces it with a puzzle: bees cannot speak, yet a forager can tell others exactly where to find flowers, and she does it with a dance. The author then illustrates how it works step by step: the figure-eight pattern, the straight middle run whose angle matches the food's angle to the sun, and the length of the waggle showing distance. This illustration connects directly to the introduction, because it answers the very question the opening raised: how a bee passes along precise directions without words.

steps: Identify the subject: the honeybee's waggle dance as a form of communication.
Find the introduction: the puzzle that wordless bees can give exact directions.
Find the illustration: the figure-eight, the angle matching the sun, and the waggle length showing distance.
Connect them: the detailed illustration answers the question the introduction posed.

Read the passage, then answer.

"When a wildfire tears through a forest, it can look like total ruin. Blackened trunks stand over gray ash, and the ground seems lifeless. Yet some forests do not merely survive fire; they depend on it. The lodgepole pine, common in the western mountains, makes cones sealed shut with a thick resin. Year after year these cones hang closed, holding their seeds in storage. Only intense heat, like the heat of a passing fire, melts the resin and lets the cones snap open, scattering seeds onto soil that the flames have just cleared of competing plants. The ash left behind even adds nutrients to that soil. Within a few seasons, a carpet of young pines can rise from ground that looked dead. In these forests, fire is not only a destroyer but also a gardener, and a forest that never burned would slowly lose the very trees that define it."

The author shifts how fire is presented from the start of the passage to the end. Explain how the treatment of fire at the end differs from how it is introduced, and how the middle connects the two.
items.answer: At the start, the author introduces fire as something that looks like total ruin: blackened trunks, gray ash, lifeless ground. By the end, fire is presented as a gardener that the forest depends on, not only a destroyer. The middle connects these opposite views by illustrating how the lodgepole pine's resin-sealed cones need fire's heat to open and scatter seeds, and how the ash even feeds the soil. This illustration deepens the introduction by explaining why the apparent ruin is actually renewal, so the ending can reverse the opening image with evidence the reader has just been given.

steps: Note the opening treatment of fire: it looks like total ruin and death.
Note the closing treatment: fire is a gardener the forest depends on.
Find the middle that links them: the lodgepole pine's heat-opened cones and the nutrient-rich ash.
Explain the connection: the middle's evidence lets the author reverse the opening image by the end.

Read the passage, then answer.

"Few people have ever heard of Henrietta Lacks, yet her cells have touched nearly every part of modern medicine. In 1951, Lacks, a young mother, went to a hospital for treatment of cancer. Without telling her, a doctor took a small sample of her cells. Most cells taken this way died quickly in the lab. Hers did not. They kept dividing again and again, the first human cells that scientists could grow without limit. Researchers named the line HeLa, after the first letters of her names. Over the following decades, HeLa cells helped test the polio vaccine, study the effects of radiation, and learn how viruses invade the body. They have been sent into space and grown in labs on every continent. For years, almost no one knew where the cells had come from, and her own family did not understand what had happened. Only much later did the world learn the name behind the cells that had quietly advanced so much research."

The passage develops the subject across stages. Choose the part that most deepens the reader's understanding of why Henrietta Lacks matters, and explain how it builds on the introduction.
items.answer: The part that most deepens the understanding is the stretch describing what HeLa cells did over the decades: they helped test the polio vaccine, study radiation, learn how viruses invade, and were even sent into space and grown on every continent. This builds directly on the introduction, which claims her cells touched nearly every part of modern medicine but does not yet prove it. The introduction makes the claim; this later part illustrates and elaborates it with specific accomplishments, turning a broad statement into a concrete case for why she matters. The detail that her cells, unlike others, kept dividing without limit links the two by explaining why hers could do so much.

steps: Identify the introduction's claim: her cells touched nearly every part of modern medicine.
Find the part that proves that claim: the list of what HeLa cells accomplished over decades.
Explain why that part deepens understanding: it gives concrete evidence for the broad opening claim.
Connect the parts: the detail that her cells divided without limit links the introduction to the later accomplishments.

Read the passage, then answer.

"A single tree standing in a field looks like a loner, but a forest is far more connected than it appears. Beneath the soil, the roots of trees are wrapped in fine threads of fungus, finer than thread and almost invisible. These threads spread for great distances, linking one tree's roots to another's. Through this hidden web, trees can pass sugar, water, and even chemical warnings to their neighbors. A tall, healthy tree can send extra sugar to a young seedling shaded beneath it, helping it survive its first years. When insects attack one tree, signals can travel the web and prompt nearby trees to raise their chemical defenses before the insects arrive. Scientists who study this network sometimes call it the 'wood wide web.' What once looked like a crowd of separate trees now looks more like a single community sharing resources underground."

The passage opens by calling a tree a 'loner' and ends by calling the forest a 'community.' Explain how the author elaborates the idea across the middle to move the reader from the first image to the second.
items.answer: The author introduces a misleading image: a tree looks like a loner. The author elaborates the true idea across the middle by illustrating the hidden fungal web that links tree roots, then giving examples of what travels through it: a tall tree sending sugar to a shaded seedling, and warning signals that prompt nearby trees to raise their defenses. Each example shows trees acting for one another, not alone. These illustrations build on each other so that by the end the author can name the forest a community sharing resources underground. The middle is what moves the reader from the loner image to the community image, because it supplies the evidence of connection.

steps: Note the opening image: a tree looks like a loner.
Note the closing image: the forest is a connected community.
Find the middle elaboration: the fungal web and the examples of sharing sugar and sending warnings.
Explain how the examples build: each shows trees helping one another, justifying the final 'community' image.

Read the passage, then answer.

"In the early 1900s, a young woman named Bessie Coleman dreamed of flying, but no flight school in the United States would admit her because she was Black and a woman. Rather than give up, she did something few would have dared. She learned French, saved money from two jobs, and sailed to France, where a famous flight school agreed to teach her. In 1921, she returned home as the first African American woman to earn an international pilot's license. Coleman could have flown quietly, but she chose a louder path. She became a stunt pilot, looping and diving before huge crowds, and she used her fame to speak out. She refused to perform at any show where Black spectators were forced to enter through a separate gate. She told audiences that she wanted to open a flight school so that other Black Americans could learn to fly. Her own life was cut short in a crash, yet the doors she pushed against did not close again so easily."

The author develops Bessie Coleman through a sequence of choices. Trace how each stage builds on the one before to develop her courage, and connect the parts.
items.answer: The author introduces Coleman as a young woman barred from flight school because she was Black and a woman. The first stage of development shows her response: she learned French, saved money, and sailed to France to train, becoming the first African American woman with an international pilot's license. The next stage builds on that by showing she chose a 'louder path' as a stunt pilot rather than flying quietly. The author deepens her courage further by adding that she refused to perform where Black spectators were segregated and that she wanted to open a flight school for others. The closing connects the stages: her life ended early, yet the doors she pushed against stayed open. Each choice builds on the last, moving from overcoming a barrier, to public daring, to using fame for others.

steps: Identify the subject: Bessie Coleman and her courage.
Find the introduction: she is barred from flight school for her race and gender.
Trace the first stage: she trains in France and earns her license.
Trace the next stages: she becomes a stunt pilot and uses her fame to fight segregation and plan a school.
Connect the stages: each choice builds on the last, and the ending shows her lasting effect.

Read the passage, then answer.

"Most people think of salt as something cheap that sits in a shaker on the table. For much of history, though, salt was so valuable that it shaped trade, taxes, and even wars. Before refrigerators, salt was the main way to keep meat and fish from rotting, so a steady supply meant the difference between eating through winter and going hungry. Cities grew up around salt mines and salt springs, and long caravans carried salt across deserts to trade for gold, weight for weight. Rulers learned they could tax salt because everyone needed it, and some governments grew rich on that tax alone. In France, a hated salt tax helped push ordinary people toward revolution. In India, centuries later, Mohandas Gandhi led a long march to the sea to make salt from ocean water, defying a British law, and that simple act became a powerful protest. What looks like an ordinary mineral has, again and again, sat at the center of human history."

The author claims salt 'shaped trade, taxes, and even wars.' Explain how the passage illustrates each of those three areas, and how the examples connect back to the opening claim.
items.answer: The author opens by claiming salt shaped trade, taxes, and even wars, then illustrates each. For trade, the author describes cities growing around salt mines and caravans carrying salt across deserts to trade for gold weight for weight. For taxes, the author explains that rulers taxed salt because everyone needed it and some governments grew rich on it. For wars and conflict, the author gives the French salt tax that pushed people toward revolution and Gandhi's salt march that defied British law. Each example connects back to the opening claim by giving concrete proof for one of the three areas, so the broad statement that salt sat at the center of human history is supported by specific cases.

steps: Identify the opening claim: salt shaped trade, taxes, and even wars.
Find the trade illustration: salt cities and caravans trading salt for gold.
Find the taxes illustration: rulers taxing salt and growing rich on it.
Find the conflict illustration: the French salt tax and Gandhi's salt march.
Connect each example back to the opening claim it proves.

"The dodo bird has become a symbol of extinction, but the real story of how it vanished is often misunderstood. The dodo lived only on Mauritius, an island in the Indian Ocean with no large predators. Over many generations, having no enemies, the bird lost the ability to fly and built its nest on the open ground. It had no reason to fear anything, so it did not flee from approaching animals. When sailors reached the island in the late 1500s, they hunted some dodos for food, and people often blame the sailors alone. Yet the ships also carried pigs, rats, monkeys, and dogs, and these animals were far more destructive. They ate the dodo's eggs and chicks straight from the unguarded nests on the ground. A bird that laid a single egg at a time could not replace its young fast enough. Within less than a century, the dodo was gone. Its disappearance was less a tale of one cause than of a creature perfectly suited to an island that suddenly changed."

The author corrects a common belief across the passage. Explain how the author moves from the introduction to a fuller, more accurate explanation, and show how the parts connect.
items.answer: The author introduces the dodo as a symbol of extinction whose real story is misunderstood, signaling a correction. The author then illustrates the bird's situation: it lived without predators, lost flight, nested on open ground, and did not flee. Next the author addresses the common belief, that sailors alone killed the dodo, and elaborates a fuller explanation: the ships also brought pigs, rats, monkeys, and dogs that ate eggs and chicks from the unguarded nests, and a bird laying one egg at a time could not recover. The parts connect because the early details about the dodo's defenseless nesting set up why the introduced animals were so destructive, leading to the corrected conclusion that the extinction had many causes, not one.

steps: Note the introduction's signal: the real story is misunderstood, so a correction is coming.
Find the illustration of the dodo's traits: no predators, no flight, ground nests, no fear.
Find the common belief named: sailors alone are blamed.
Find the fuller explanation: introduced animals ate eggs and chicks, and the slow-breeding bird could not recover.
Connect the parts: the dodo's defenseless nesting explains why the new animals doomed it.

Read the passage, then answer.

"Long before the internet, people dreamed of a machine that could think. In the 1830s, an English mathematician named Charles Babbage designed a giant mechanical calculator he called the Analytical Engine. It was built of gears and rods and was meant to be fed instructions on punched cards. Babbage never finished building it, but a young woman named Ada Lovelace saw further than he did. Lovelace studied his design closely and wrote a long set of notes about it. In those notes, she did something remarkable: she wrote out a step-by-step method the machine could follow to calculate a series of numbers. Most people, including Babbage, thought of the engine only as a fast calculator for arithmetic. Lovelace argued that it could do far more. If numbers could stand for other things, like musical notes, she suggested, then the machine might one day compose music or handle any kind of information, not just sums. For this vision, written more than a century before modern computers, she is often called the first computer programmer."

The passage develops two connected individuals, Babbage and Lovelace. Explain how the author uses Babbage to set up Lovelace, and how the later part deepens her importance beyond his.
items.answer: The author first introduces Babbage and his Analytical Engine, a mechanical calculator he designed but never finished. This sets up Lovelace, because the author then shows she 'saw further than he did.' The author illustrates her contribution by explaining that she wrote a step-by-step method the machine could follow, an early program. The later part deepens her importance beyond Babbage's by contrasting their visions: most people, including Babbage, saw only a fast calculator, but Lovelace argued it could handle any information and even compose music if numbers stood for other things. The parts connect because Babbage's narrower view becomes the measure against which Lovelace's larger vision stands out, leading to her title as the first computer programmer.

steps: Identify the two individuals: Babbage and Lovelace.
Show how Babbage is introduced first: his unfinished Analytical Engine.
Find the setup line: Lovelace 'saw further than he did.'
Find the deepening contrast: Babbage saw a calculator; Lovelace saw a machine for any information.
Connect the parts: Babbage's narrower view makes Lovelace's vision stand out.

"At first glance, a desert seems like the last place a frog could live. Deserts can go months, even years, without a drop of rain, and a frog's thin skin loses water quickly. Yet the water-holding frog of Australia not only survives the desert; it has turned the desert's harshness into a strange advantage. When rain finally falls, the frog drinks until its body swells like a balloon, storing water in its bladder and beneath its skin. Then it digs backward into the mud, deeper than a hand can reach, and seals itself inside a cocoon made of its own shed skin. There it waits, barely breathing, sometimes for years, living off its stored water. When the next heavy rain soaks down to its chamber, the frog wakes, climbs to the surface, and races to breed in the brief pools before they dry. Desert peoples once dug up these frogs and gently squeezed them for an emergency drink of water. A creature that should not belong in the desert has become one of its quiet experts at survival."

The author opens by saying a desert 'seems like the last place a frog could live' and closes by calling the frog 'one of its quiet experts at survival.' Trace how the body of the passage develops the subject to bridge those two statements.
items.answer: The author introduces a contradiction: a desert seems like the last place a frog could live because deserts lack rain and a frog loses water fast. The body bridges to the closing claim by illustrating, in stages, how the water-holding frog survives. First it drinks until it swells and stores water in its bladder and skin. Then it digs backward into the mud and seals itself in a cocoon of shed skin. Then it waits, barely breathing, for years until rain returns, when it wakes and races to breed. Each stage builds on the last to show a creature perfectly adapted to drought. These elaborations earn the closing statement, because the frog's stored water and cocoon explain how something that 'should not belong' became an expert at desert survival.

steps: Note the opening contradiction: a frog seems unable to live in a desert.
Note the closing claim: the frog is a quiet expert at survival.
Trace the body's stages: drinking and swelling, burrowing and forming a cocoon, waiting for years, then breeding.
Show the stages build on one another to reveal a deeply adapted survivor.
Connect to the close: the adaptations justify calling the frog a desert expert.

Read the passage, then answer.

"In the winter of 1925, the small town of Nome, Alaska, faced a deadly outbreak of a disease called diphtheria, and the only medicine that could stop it was nearly a thousand miles away. Nome was icebound; no ship could reach it, and the few airplanes of the time could not fly safely in the brutal cold and dark. The town's doctor sent an urgent plea by telegraph. Officials settled on a daring plan: relay the medicine by dog sled. Teams of sled dogs and their drivers, called mushers, would carry the serum across the frozen wilderness, each team running a stretch of the route before handing the package to the next. Through blizzards and temperatures far below zero, the dogs pressed on. A lead dog named Balto guided the final team into Nome through a storm so fierce the musher could barely see his own animals. The serum arrived in time, and the outbreak was stopped. The relay, later called the Great Race of Mercy, showed how a chain of separate teams, each doing its part, could accomplish what no single team could have done alone."

The author develops the event of the 1925 serum run. Explain how the author moves from the problem to the solution, and how the final sentence connects the parts into one idea.
items.answer: The author introduces the event as a problem: Nome faces a deadly diphtheria outbreak, and the only medicine is nearly a thousand miles away, with the town icebound and planes unable to fly. The author then develops the solution in stages: officials choose a dog sled relay, teams of dogs and mushers each run a stretch and hand off the serum, they press through blizzards and extreme cold, and the lead dog Balto guides the final team into Nome through a storm. The author elaborates the outcome: the serum arrives in time and the outbreak is stopped. The final sentence connects all the parts into one idea by naming what the relay showed: a chain of separate teams, each doing its part, accomplished what no single team could have done alone. That sentence ties the introduction's problem to the solution's relay structure.

steps: Identify the event: the 1925 serum run to Nome.
Find the problem introduction: a deadly outbreak and medicine almost a thousand miles away with no way in.
Trace the solution: the dog sled relay, the handoffs, the blizzards, and Balto's final run.
Find the outcome: the serum arrives and the outbreak is stopped.
Explain the final sentence: it unites the parts by stating the lesson of the relay.

"It is easy to assume that a thing is named after the person who invented it, but in science that is often not true. Take the word 'pasteurization,' the process of heating milk to kill harmful germs. It is named for Louis Pasteur, and he did help prove that germs spoil food. Yet the basic idea of heating drinks to preserve them was used long before him. Or consider Halley's Comet, named for the astronomer Edmond Halley. Halley did not discover the comet; people had recorded its visits for centuries. What he did was calculate that several past sightings were the same comet returning, and he predicted its next appearance. The name honors his prediction, not a discovery. Even the Americas, two whole continents, are named for the mapmaker Amerigo Vespucci rather than for the sailors who first reached them. These examples reveal a pattern: a name often marks the person who explained or popularized an idea, not the one who first stumbled upon it. A label, it turns out, can tell us less about who was first than about who made the world understand."

The author develops one central idea through a series of examples. State the idea, then explain how each example illustrates it and how the parts build toward the conclusion.
items.answer: The central idea is that things in science are often named not for whoever was first, but for the person who explained or popularized an idea. The author illustrates this with three examples that build on one another. Pasteurization is named for Pasteur, though heating drinks to preserve them was used before him; he proved the germ idea. Halley's Comet is named for Halley, who did not discover it but calculated that past sightings were the same comet and predicted its return. The Americas are named for Vespucci, a mapmaker, not the sailors who first arrived. Each example adds another case of the same pattern, and the author connects them in the conclusion: a name marks who made the world understand an idea, not who first stumbled on it. The parts build from a single field to two continents, widening the pattern before stating it plainly.

steps: State the central idea: names often honor who explained or popularized, not who was first.
Find the first example: pasteurization and Pasteur, who proved but did not originate the idea.
Find the second example: Halley's Comet, named for a prediction, not a discovery.
Find the third example: the Americas, named for a mapmaker.
Explain the build: the examples widen in scale and all show the same pattern, leading to the conclusion.

"A coral reef can look like a colorful garden of rock, but it is built by living creatures so small they are easy to miss. Each tiny animal, called a polyp, is no bigger than a pencil eraser and looks a little like a soft, see-through flower. What makes the reef possible is a quiet partnership. Inside the polyp's body live even smaller algae, and these algae use sunlight to make food, sharing much of it with their host. In return, the polyp gives the algae a safe place to live. Fed by this partnership, each polyp builds a hard cup of limestone around itself. Generation after generation, new polyps grow on the limestone left by the old, and over thousands of years their cups pile into the vast stone structures we call reefs. Those reefs then shelter a quarter of all ocean species, from tiny fish to sharks. When the water grows too warm, though, the algae leave, the polyps lose their food, and the reef can starve and turn a ghostly white. The whole bright world of the reef, it turns out, rests on a tiny animal and the partner hidden inside it."

The author develops the subject of the coral reef from the smallest scale to the largest. Trace how the author builds from a single polyp to a vast reef and explain how the final sentence ties the parts together.
items.answer: The author introduces the reef as a colorful garden of rock built by creatures too small to notice, then narrows to the single polyp, an animal no bigger than a pencil eraser. The author illustrates the key partnership: algae living inside the polyp make food by sunlight and share it, while the polyp gives them a safe home. Fed by this, each polyp builds a limestone cup. The author then elaborates the scale upward: new polyps grow on the limestone of the old, and over thousands of years the cups pile into vast reefs that shelter a quarter of ocean species. The author adds a warning stage: when water warms, the algae leave and the reef can starve and bleach white. The final sentence ties the parts together by returning to the smallest scale, stating that the whole bright reef rests on a tiny animal and its hidden partner, linking the largest result back to its smallest cause.

steps: Identify the subject: the coral reef and how it is built.
Find the introduction and narrowing: the reef built by tiny polyps, then a single polyp.
Find the partnership illustration: algae feeding the polyp, the polyp sheltering the algae.
Trace the build upward: limestone cups piling over thousands of years into vast reefs sheltering many species.
Note the warning stage: warming drives algae out and the reef bleaches.
Explain the final sentence: it returns to the smallest scale, tying the huge reef back to the tiny polyp and its partner.
